description: The ten functional properties of carbohydrates, fats, proteins and fruit and vegetables when cooked.
content_html:
Why Ingredients Behave the Way They Do

Every time you make a sauce, bake a cake or fry an egg, you are running a chemistry experiment. The spec identifies ten functional properties — specific chemical or physical changes that occur when ingredients are subjected to heat, liquid, mechanical action or acid. Knowing the correct term, the right ingredient and what happens at a molecular level is the difference between a one-mark recall answer and an eight-mark explanation. This lesson covers all ten, grouped by ingredient type, focusing on familiar dishes and what goes wrong when they fail.

Carbohydrates: Gelatinisation and Dextrinization

Gelatinisation is what happens to starch in a liquid when heated above approximately 60°C. Starch exists as tightly packed granules containing two types of starch molecule: amylose (long straight chains) and amylopectin (branched chains). When the granule is placed in warm liquid and heated, the hydrogen bonds holding the granule together weaken, water molecules force their way in, and the granule swells dramatically. Above about 80°C, the granule bursts, releasing the amylose and amylopectin molecules into the surrounding liquid. These molecules form a tangled network that traps water — the result is the thickening of a sauce, custard, gravy or soup. As the mixture cools, the network becomes more rigid; a cornflour-thickened pudding sets solid in the fridge because the starch molecules form a firm gel on cooling.

A common failure: a lumpy sauce. If starch is added directly to hot liquid, the outer granules gelatinise instantly and form a sticky coating that traps dry starch inside. The fix is to disperse starch in cold liquid or fat first (a slurry or roux), then heat gradually while stirring.

Dextrinization occurs when starch is subjected to dry heat rather than moist heat. The long starch chains are broken by heat into shorter fragments called dextrins. These are sweeter than raw starch, browner in colour and more soluble. The golden-brown crust on toasted bread, the crust on a baked pastry, the coating on roasted potatoes and the surface of a pan of fried rice all involve dextrinization. Unlike gelatinisation (which requires water), dextrinization requires only heat and the absence of water — that is why bread goes golden in a toaster but not in a bowl of water.

Both involve starch and both involve heat, so students conflate them. The key distinction: gelatinisation = starch + water + heat — granules swell and burst, thickening a liquid (a sauce, a custard, a gravy). Dextrinization = starch + dry heat (no water) — starch chains break into dextrins, causing browning and a sweetened, crisped surface (toast crust, pastry crust, roasted potato skin). A bechamel sauce thickening on the hob is gelatinisation. The pastry case turning golden in the oven is dextrinization. They cannot both be the same process because one requires water and the other requires the absence of it.

Fats and Oils: Shortening, Aeration, Plasticity and Emulsification

Shortening occurs when fat coats the flour protein particles, preventing the glutenin and gliadin from combining with water to form gluten. The result is a product with a crumbly, tender, “short” texture. Shortcrust pastry and shortbread both exploit shortening: rubbing cold butter into flour coats the flour in fat before any water is added, limiting gluten formation and giving the characteristic melt-in-the-mouth crumb. The fat is literally “shortening” the gluten network.

Aeration is the incorporation of air bubbles into fat during creaming or whisking. When softened butter and sugar are beaten together (as in the creaming method for a Victoria sandwich), the sugar crystals cut through the fat, creating tiny air pockets that are trapped in the fat. In the oven, these air bubbles expand as the temperature rises, helping the cake to rise and develop a light, open crumb. Without adequate aeration during creaming, the cake will be dense and heavy — a common cause of a sunken, flat sponge.

Plasticity describes the spreadability and workability of solid fats at room temperature. Butter and margarine are plastic: they can be spread, rolled into pastry, shaped and piped because their crystal structure deforms without crumbling. Lard is highly plastic and was traditionally used for pastry, producing particularly short, crumbly results.

Emulsification is the process of combining an oil and a water-based liquid into a stable mixture. Normally, oil and water separate because their molecules are structurally incompatible. An emulsifier has one end that is attracted to water (hydrophilic) and one end attracted to fat (lipophilic). Lecithin in egg yolk is the natural emulsifier in mayonnaise: as the yolk is whisked with vinegar and oil is drizzled in slowly, the lecithin molecules surround tiny oil droplets, keeping them suspended in the vinegar. Remove the egg yolk or add the oil too quickly, and the emulsion splits — the oil and vinegar separate out.

Proteins: Coagulation, Foam Formation, Gluten Formation and Denaturation

Coagulation is the irreversible setting of protein after it has been denatured. When an egg is heated, the protein molecules (albumin in the white, phosvitin and livetin in the yolk) unfold (denature) and then bond together to form a solid network. A perfectly scrambled egg coagulates gently at around 70–80°C, forming soft, creamy curds. Overcooked, it becomes rubbery because excessive heat causes too many cross-links between molecules, squeezing out water. Coagulation also sets the crumb of a cake (egg protein sets around the air bubbles), thickens a custard and firms the interior of a quiche.

Foam formation occurs when egg whites are whisked. Physical action denatures the albumin proteins, causing them to partially unfold and form a film around the air bubbles introduced by whisking. Continuing to whisk builds the foam from soft peaks to stiff peaks. Fat in any form (even a trace of yolk) inhibits foam formation because it coats the protein molecules and prevents them forming a stable film — bowls and whisks must be completely fat-free for meringue.

Gluten formation occurs when wheat flour is mixed with water. Two proteins in the flour — glutenin (strong, elastic) and gliadin (extensible, plastic) — absorb water and link together to form gluten strands. Kneading develops and aligns these strands into a strong, elastic network that can trap carbon dioxide bubbles from yeast fermentation, allowing bread dough to rise and hold its shape during baking. The more a dough is kneaded, the stronger and more elastic the gluten network. Conversely, for shortcrust pastry, gluten development is minimised by using cold fat, cold water and minimal mixing — too much gluten makes pastry tough and difficult to roll.

Denaturation can be caused by heat (cooking an egg), acid (lime juice “cooking” fish in a ceviche — acid denaturation) or physical action (whisking egg whites). Importantly, denaturation is the first step before coagulation — protein first unfolds, then sets. Understanding the distinction matters: a gently warmed egg may partially denature without fully coagulating; an overheated scrambled egg fully coagulates to a rubbery solid.

Key Fact

Ten functional properties to know: Carbohydrates — gelatinisation (sauce thickening), dextrinization (bread crust). Fats/oils — shortening (pastry crumb), aeration (cake rising), plasticity (butter spreading), emulsification (mayonnaise). Protein — coagulation (scrambled eggs setting), foam formation (meringue), gluten formation (bread structure), denaturation (egg white changing on heat).

Key Fact

The emulsifier in egg yolk is lecithin — it has a hydrophilic (water-attracting) end and a lipophilic (fat-attracting) end, which is why mayonnaise holds its oil-in-water structure. Just one drop of yolk in an egg-white foam collapses it, because the fat in the yolk coats the albumin proteins before they can form a stable film around the air bubbles.

Fruit and Vegetables: Enzymic Browning and Oxidisation

Enzymic browning occurs when fruit or vegetables are cut, bruised or damaged. Cells in the produce contain polyphenol oxidase enzymes that are normally kept separate from the phenolic compounds (substrates) also in the tissue. When the cells are disrupted, the enzyme and substrate come into contact, and in the presence of oxygen, a chemical reaction produces brown-coloured melanin pigments. This is why a sliced apple, a cut avocado, a peeled banana or a raw potato turns brown when left exposed to air. To prevent enzymic browning: coat the cut surface with lemon juice or ascorbic acid (vitamin C, which acts as an antioxidant competing for the oxygen), submerge in cold water (limiting oxygen contact), blanch briefly (heat deactivates the enzyme), or refrigerate (cold slows the enzymatic reaction).

Oxidisation is a broader chemical process in which oxygen reacts with food components, causing deterioration. In vegetables, oxidisation of chlorophyll causes colour loss — overcooked broccoli turns dull and khaki as the pigment degrades. Oxidisation of vitamin C during prolonged cooking also reduces nutritional value. In fats, oxidisation causes rancidity — the unpleasant smell and taste of stale cooking oil or old butter. Minimising oxygen exposure through airtight packaging, refrigeration or vacuum packing slows oxidisation in storage.

A sponge cake that sinks in the middle after baking is a classic functional-properties exam scenario. The most likely causes: insufficient aeration during the creaming stage — if the butter was too cold or the creaming time too short, not enough air bubbles were incorporated; too much raising agent — excess carbon dioxide from baking powder creates large bubbles that the protein and starch network cannot support before it has set, so the cake rises then collapses; opening the oven door too early — the cold air rush causes the structure to collapse before the egg protein has fully coagulated; under-baking — starch has not fully gelatinised and egg protein has not fully coagulated, leaving the centre too liquid to hold its shape as the cake cools. The remedy: use butter at room temperature, cream thoroughly until pale and doubled in volume, avoid opening the oven for the first 15 minutes, and check the centre with a skewer before removing.
exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark Discuss or Analyse question on functional properties, the most common error is describing only one or two functional changes without analysing connections between them or considering what happens when they go wrong. A top-band Mastering response names specific functional properties using the exact spec vocabulary (do not write “the egg sets” when “coagulation” is the precise term), links each property to the dish or scenario in the question, explains the underlying physical or chemical mechanism (even briefly), and analyses a failure mode — why the property might not work as intended and how to remedy it. For example, in a question on a Victoria sandwich: name aeration (butter-sugar creaming traps air), link to the light crumb, explain that insufficient creaming fails to incorporate enough air, and connect this to the cake sinking. The command words “Discuss” and “Analyse” require multiple perspectives — aim for at least two functional properties clearly explored, not a list of six half-explained ones.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Ten functional properties to know: gelatinisation and dextrinization (carbohydrates); shortening, aeration, plasticity and emulsification (fats/oils); coagulation, foam formation, gluten formation and denaturation (proteins); enzymic browning and oxidisation (fruit/vegetables).
  • Gelatinisation (starch + water + heat → thickened sauce) is distinct from dextrinization (starch + dry heat → golden-brown crust). Coagulation (protein sets irreversibly) follows denaturation (protein unfolds) and cannot be reversed.
  • When desired results are not achieved — a sinking sponge, a lumpy sauce, a split emulsion, enzymic browning on cut apples — there is always a functional-properties explanation. Identifying the property, explaining the failure mechanism and proposing a remedy is exactly what high-tariff exam questions require.

practice_questions.text:
Which functional property of starch is responsible for a white sauce thickening as it heats on the hob?
A) Dextrinization
B) Coagulation
C) Gelatinisation
D) Emulsification
Name the two proteins in wheat flour that combine with water to form gluten.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for both correct: glutenin and gliadin. Both must be named for the mark.

practice_questions.text: State two ways a cook could prevent enzymic browning on freshly cut avocado.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correct, distinct method, up to 2 marks. Acceptable answers: coat the cut surface with lemon juice or lime juice (the vitamin C/ascorbic acid acts as an antioxidant); submerge in cold water to limit oxygen contact; cover with cling film pressed directly onto the surface to exclude air; refrigerate (cold slows the enzyme action); blanch briefly in boiling water (heat denatures the polyphenol oxidase enzyme). Do not credit 'put in the fridge' without mentioning the mechanism for full marks; accept 'coat in citric acid'.

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens at a molecular level when egg whites are whisked to form a meringue foam.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each distinct, accurate point, up to 3 marks. Acceptable answers: physical action (whisking) partially denatures the albumin proteins in the egg white, causing them to unfold (1); the unfolded proteins form a film around the air bubbles introduced by the whisk, trapping them (1); as whisking continues, the protein network strengthens and stiffens to hold the foam at soft then stiff peaks (1); any fat (e.g. egg yolk) prevents foam formation because it coats the protein molecules and stops them forming a stable film (1). Credit clear reference to denaturation plus air entrapment plus protein film.

practice_questions.text: Zara is making a pastry case for a savoury quiche. Her first attempt produced pastry that shrank in the tin and came out tough and chewy. Using your knowledge of gluten formation and shortening, explain what most likely went wrong and how she should change her technique.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 1 mark for each correctly identified problem + 1 mark for the linked remedy explanation. Tough/chewy pastry most likely indicates overdeveloped gluten: Zara probably added too much water (1) which allowed glutenin and gliadin to combine fully and form a strong gluten network (1); or she overworked (over-mixed or over-kneaded) the dough (1) which strengthened and aligned the gluten strands further, making the pastry elastic and resistant (1). Remedy: use cold butter and cold water; add water gradually in small amounts; stop mixing as soon as the dough just comes together; rest the pastry in the fridge for 20-30 minutes before rolling (resting relaxes the gluten network) (1 mark for a specific, accurate remedy with a because-link). Shrinking also suggests the gluten network is too tight — resting resolves this (1). Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Analyse the functional properties involved when making a Victoria sandwich, and discuss what could go wrong at each stage and how the problems could be fixed.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Clear identification and accurate explanation of at least four functional properties relevant to a Victoria sandwich — aeration (creaming butter and sugar to trap air, which expands in the oven for a light crumb), gelatinisation (flour starch absorbs liquid and sets structure in the oven), coagulation (egg protein coagulates to set the crumb permanently), and potentially dextrinization (golden crust on the outside). For each, a failure mode is identified with an accurate cause-and-effect explanation and a practical remedy. Multiple perspectives analysed — e.g. aeration failure vs gluten over-development vs under-baking. Accurate use of functional-property vocabulary throughout. Both the 'what goes right' and 'what goes wrong' sides are developed.

Secure (5-6 marks): Three or four properties named with mostly accurate explanations; failure modes present but not all fully developed; at least one remedy given; cause-and-effect chains mostly complete; vocabulary generally accurate.

Developing (3-4 marks): Two properties identified with limited explanation; one failure mode mentioned but mechanism vague; remedy listed without explaining why it works; may describe the process without using functional-property terms.

Emerging (1-2 marks): General statements about baking with little use of functional-property vocabulary; one stage described; no failure modes or remedies.

knowledge_checks.q: Which functional property describes fat coating flour particles and preventing full gluten development, resulting in a crumbly pastry?
Enzymic browning is caused by polyphenol oxidase enzymes reacting with oxygen when cells in fruit or vegetables are _____ or bruised.
Dextrinization requires _____ heat (not water) to break starch chains into shorter, sweeter, browner dextrins.
During foam formation, the _____ proteins in egg white denature and form a film around the air bubbles introduced by whisking.
Match each functional property to the correct ingredient and dish example:
right: Starch granules swelling in liquid above 60 °C — thickens a white sauce
Egg yolk lecithin keeping oil droplets suspended in vinegar — mayonnaise
Egg proteins setting irreversibly on heating — scrambled eggs

flashcard_questions.a: Starch granules absorb water and swell above 60 °C, then burst to release starch molecules that form a gel, thickening the liquid.
Starch broken down by dry heat into shorter dextrin chains — sweeter, more soluble and golden-brown (e.g. toast crust, pastry crust).
Fat coating flour particles and preventing gluten development, producing a crumbly, tender texture in pastry and biscuits.

flashcard_questions.q: What is aeration in the context of fat?
flashcard_questions.a: Fat trapping air bubbles during creaming or beating, contributing to a light, risen texture in cakes.
The ability of solid fats to be spread, shaped or moulded without crumbling due to their semi-solid crystal structure.
Combining two normally immiscible liquids (oil and water) into a stable mixture using an emulsifier such as lecithin in egg yolk.
The irreversible setting of denatured protein molecules into a solid or semi-solid network — e.g. scrambled eggs setting when heated.
Egg white albumin proteins partially denature during whisking and form a film around air bubbles, creating a stable foam.
Glutenin and gliadin proteins in wheat flour combine with water and kneading to form an elastic gluten network that traps gas and structures dough.
Polyphenol oxidase enzymes in cut fruit or vegetables react with oxygen to produce brown melanin pigments.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two ways to prevent enzymic browning on cut apple or avocado.
flashcard_questions.a: Coat with lemon juice (ascorbic acid competes for oxygen); or submerge in cold water to limit oxygen contact.

flashcard_questions.q: Why would a trace of egg yolk prevent egg whites from forming a stiff meringue foam?
flashcard_questions.a: Egg yolk fat coats the albumin proteins and prevents them from forming the stable protein film needed to trap air bubbles.

glossary_terms.definition: The process in which starch granules absorb water and swell when heated above 60 °C, eventually bursting to release starch molecules that form a gel-like network, thickening the liquid.
The process in which starch is broken down by dry heat into shorter dextrin molecules that are sweeter, more soluble and golden-brown in colour.
The property of fat that coats flour particles, preventing full gluten development, resulting in a crumbly, tender texture in pastry and biscuits.
The ability of fat or butter to trap air bubbles during creaming or beating, contributing to a light, risen texture in baked goods.
The process of combining two normally immiscible liquids (such as oil and water) into a stable mixture using an emulsifier such as lecithin.
The irreversible process by which denatured protein molecules aggregate and form a solid or semi-solid network, setting the structure of the food.
The process in which egg white albumin proteins partially denature during whisking and form a film around air bubbles, creating a stable foam.
The formation of a stretchy, elastic protein network when glutenin and gliadin proteins in wheat flour combine with water and are developed by kneading.
A chemical reaction in which polyphenol oxidase enzymes in cut or bruised fruit and vegetables react with oxygen to produce brown-coloured compounds.
The process by which a protein's three-dimensional structure is disrupted by heat, acid or physical action, changing its properties.
